rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate the six-peak elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.
The first method already achieves the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient while holding temperature and endpoints fixed to test whether full resolution can be retained in less time.
Shorten the gradient another step to seek a faster method with the same maximum CRF. The closest pair still has resolution 2.46, leaving some margin for further compression.

The 4-minute gradient retains maximum CRF but leaves little resolution margin for the first pair. Raise temperature to test whether favorable selectivity permits a shorter elution time without losing full resolution.

Heating worsened the critical first-pair separation, so test the lowest temperature to gain selectivity while shortening the gradient to its minimum duration. This probes a faster candidate while retaining injection 3 as a proven maximum-CRF method.

Reduce gradient steepness at the lowest temperature to improve the first pair toward R ≥ 1.5 while keeping the 2-minute gradient. The last peak may elute during the final hold, so this tests the trade-off between early-pair resolution and late retention.

Shift the narrow gradient window upward to retain a shallow slope while restoring a strong final solvent that elutes the last peak quickly. This tests whether the first pair remains resolved despite reduced initial retention.

Increase the starting organic fraction one step to narrow the gradient further and potentially improve the critical pair while shortening late retention. Monitor the first peaks for compression as they approach the unretained region.

Raise the starting organic fraction one more step to test whether the narrower gradient further improves resolution and shortens elution. The first peak is approaching the unretained region, so this probes the practical upper limit for phi0.
Increase temperature by one step to shorten late retention while testing the first pair’s remaining resolution margin. Keep the gradient unchanged to isolate temperature-dependent selectivity.

Test whether a narrower, higher-starting gradient can shorten the run while retaining maximum CRF. This also checks the onset of early-peak compression, since the first peak is already close to the unretained region.

Return to phi0 0.30 to avoid the early-peak compression seen at 0.35, and test one temperature step above the fastest fully resolved method. This checks the upper temperature boundary for retaining maximum CRF.

Narrow the gradient at 35 C to recover first-pair resolution while retaining the minimum gradient duration. The stronger retention during the final hold will reveal whether this selectivity gain comes with an acceptable increase in last-peak time.

Lower the starting organic fraction to move the first pair away from the unretained region, where reducing slope alone gave little improvement. This tests whether full resolution can be recovered at 35 C with a 2-minute gradient.

Reduce the final organic fraction one step to make the gradient shallower and lift the first pair from R 1.42 toward full resolution. Injection 10 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method; this tests an alternative at higher temperature.

Refine around injection 10, the fastest fully resolved method, by slightly reducing gradient steepness to seek more first-pair resolution margin. This should incur only a modest late-retention penalty compared with the lower final organic fractions tested at 35 C.

Test a nearby maximum-CRF candidate with more early retention than injection 16 and stronger low-temperature selectivity. The slightly shallower gradient than injection 8 should improve the critical-pair margin while keeping the last peak near 3 minutes.

Raise temperature one step from injection 17 to shorten retention while testing whether its first-pair margin remains sufficient. This explores a fully resolved alternative with early peaks farther from the unretained region than injection 10.

The maximum CRF is already secured, with injection 10 the fastest fully resolved method demonstrated. Test a shallower gradient with a trimmed starting window to seek a larger resolution margin while keeping all peaks comfortably within 10 minutes.

Refine around the fastest maximum-CRF methods by combining low-temperature selectivity with a slightly shallower 2-minute gradient. This should improve the critical-pair margin relative to injection 16 while keeping late retention near 3 minutes.

Test one step shallower than injection 17 to increase the first-pair resolution margin while maintaining useful initial retention. The final solvent should still elute all six compounds well within the 10-minute no-penalty window.

Raise temperature one step from injection 21 to reduce late retention while using its first-pair resolution margin. This should provide another maximum-CRF candidate between the tested 25 C and borderline 35 C methods.

Raise phi0 one step from injection 22 to shorten retention while testing whether full first-pair resolution is preserved. Injection 10 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method; this checks a nearby alternative with a shallower gradient.

Lower temperature one step from injection 23 to increase the critical-pair resolution margin while keeping the minimum gradient duration. This nearby candidate should retain maximum CRF, though injection 10 remains the fastest fully resolved method demonstrated.

Use the final injection to test a nearby candidate expected to improve the first-pair margin over injection 22 while keeping all peaks well within 10 minutes. Maximum CRF is already secured; injection 10 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method.
